strengths: Ambitious and unified end-to-end framework that combines multi-view inverse rendering (MVSplat), transformer-based particle dynamics (extended PTv3), and 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering, trained directly on next-frame image reconstruction without requiring depth, particle tracks, or hand-crafted graph features.

Introduces a plausible methodological extension to PTv3 for temporal point clouds: temporally serialized point cloud codes, learned timestep embeddings, and temporal merging that allows attention across adjacent timesteps while reusing the same attention block.

Provides three synthetic multi-view video datasets (rigid, elastic, cloth) and extensive ablations over rollout length, camera setup, segmentation masks, modality configurations, grid resolution, and temporal merger design.

Qualitative results show promising behavior across rigid, elastic, cloth-like dynamics, shadows, multi-body interactions, and scene edits, suggesting the approach can capture diverse physical phenomena and is fast enough for practical exploration.
weaknesses: The paper's central claim—that replacing GNN/kNN graph biases with a transformer-over-space-filling-curves dynamics engine is beneficial—is not empirically supported. There is no quantitative comparison against the key particle-based simulator baselines (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys, or adapted GNN-based methods). The only baseline, Cosmos, is a single-view, language-prompted, pretrained video model and is explicitly not directly comparable, so it cannot validate the architectural contribution.

The evaluation contains metric/table inconsistencies that raise concerns about correctness. Table 11 has apparently duplicate or ambiguous rows for '3DGSim 4-12 latent' in the Elastic section, and the column 'PSNR (latent)' is not clearly defined relative to future/past prediction. More importantly, reported LPIPS values for 3DGSim are very high (~0.82–0.89) and substantially worse than Cosmos (~0.14–0.24), yet the paper highlights PSNR/SSIM and does not discuss this contradiction or explain the LPIPS scale/direction.

Evaluation is entirely on small synthetic datasets: six objects per dataset, less than six minutes of video per object, generated with simulators and known multi-view camera setups. There is no real-world validation and no detail on how camera poses are obtained, while the method depends on calibrated multi-view images. This limits the significance for the robotics motivation and leaves real-world generalization unsupported.

Several methodological claims need clearer validation. For example, temporal merging merges consecutive pairs via bit shifts, but the paper claims handling of an arbitrary number of timesteps while training with T in {2,4}; the 'view-independent' claim of the FiLM-based feature encoder is not quantitatively ablated; and the roles/pretraining status of MVSplat and the learned Gaussian head are somewhat underspecified.

Generalization claims to unseen multi-body interactions, scene edits, ground removal, and shadow modeling are supported only qualitatively. There are no quantitative metrics, failure cases, or ablations isolating whether these behaviors come from learned physics or from rendering/appearance cues.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code and datasets are only promised, not available, and no baseline implementations are released. Combined with missing implementation details and the apparent table errors, it is difficult for others to reliably build on or reproduce the claimed results.

Some claims are overextended: for cloth data recorded at 42 FPS, inference at ~16 FPS is not near real-time, and the statement that 3DGSim 'simulates elastic cloth at 42 FPS' with ~16 FPS inference may mislead readers about simulation speed.

strengths: The paper presents a genuinely novel end-to-end differentiable framework (3DGSim) that unifies feed-forward inverse rendering (MVSplat), transformer-based particle dynamics, and 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering under a single image-reconstruction loss. Integrating these three components into one trainable pipeline is a non-trivial engineering and research contribution.

The temporal merging mechanism (Section 4.3, Eq. 7) is a clever, memory-efficient idea: by right-shifting the temporal bits of the serialized point-cloud code, points from adjacent timesteps can be grouped into shared patches so the same attention block is reused across time, avoiding the per-timestep module proliferation of prior work like HD-VPD.

The ablation study (Appendix B) is fairly thorough, covering rollout length, camera setup, segmentation masks, modality configurations, grid resolution, and temporal merger strides, giving useful insight into which design choices matter (e.g., learned positional embeddings, merge timing).

The limitations section (Section 6) is honest about the reliance on multi-view data, lack of real-world validation, and lack of occlusion handling, and the qualitative visualizations of rigid, elastic cloth, shadows, and multi-body interactions are suggestive of promising behavior.
weaknesses: There is no quantitative comparison to any prior particle-based simulator (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys). The authors state these lack public code/data, but this means the paper's central claim - that a transformer-only, SFC-based dynamics engine can replace GNN/kNN-based PBS and scale better - is not empirically tested against the most relevant class of baselines. The only baseline is Cosmos, which the authors themselves admit is 'not directly comparable' (single-view video generation).

The reported metrics are internally inconsistent and unexplained. 3DGSim attains high PSNR/SSIM but very poor LPIPS (0.82-0.89) whereas Cosmos attains far better LPIPS (0.14-0.58). A PSNR of ~33 with LPIPS of ~0.82 is anomalous, and the paper neither discusses nor diagnoses this, undermining confidence in the validity of the reported numbers.

Table 11 contains errors and contradicts the text. The Elastic block lists '3DGSim 4-12 latent' multiple times (duplicate rows), and the text claims 'explicit representations achieve similar performance' whereas the table shows explicit PSNR 27.88 vs latent 20.28 on the rigid dataset - a substantial, unexplained discrepancy that directly contradicts the stated narrative.

The headline generalization claims (Section 5.2: multi-body interactions, scene edits, ground removal, running 180 steps) are supported only qualitatively via figures/videos and receive no quantitative metrics, so the 'rigorous test' framing is not backed by evidence.

Reproducibility is limited: the three datasets are custom-built, not yet released, no baseline code/data is available, and training takes ~5 days on a single H100. With only 12% of trajectories held out and less than 6 minutes of footage per object, the evidential base for generalization claims is thin.

Presentation problems reduce clarity: typos ('3DGSim is build', 'explicitely', 'for out scene size'), mismatched table captions/labels (Table S1/S2 captions do not match their content), and inconsistent baseline naming (Cosmos-1.0-Autoregressive-5B in Section 5.1 vs Cosmos-Predict2 2B in Table 11).

strengths: End-to-end differentiable framework jointly trains multi-view RGB inverse rendering, latent particle dynamics, and Gaussian-splat rendering, enabling next-image supervision without depth, particle tracks, or object-level trajectory labels.

The dynamics architecture is a meaningful extension of PTv3 to spatiotemporal point clouds: temporal serialization, learned time-step embeddings, temporal merging, and SFC-based patch attention eliminate kNN/graph construction and hand-crafted edge features.

The paper demonstrates diverse qualitative physical behaviors across rigid, elastic, and cloth datasets, including implicit cloth-corner constraints and some generalization to multi-body interactions and scene edits.
Detailed ablations on rollout length, camera setup, segmentation masks, modality configurations, grid resolution, and temporal merging provide useful insight into the design choices.
Efficiency is promising for robotics-oriented simulation: reported ~16-20 FPS inference, 12/42 FPS dataset simulation speeds, and <20 GB VRAM on an H100.
Reproducibility effort is apparent: implementation details, hyperparameters, and training setup are provided, and code/datasets are promised for release.
The limitations discussion is honest about multi-view data requirements, lack of real-world validation, and future action conditioning.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning physically accurate simulators is not directly validated: evaluation is almost entirely image-space PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, with no physical-state metrics, trajectory error, collision accuracy, conservation-law checks, or boundary-condition satisfaction metrics.

Baseline comparison is weak: the only quantitative baseline is Cosmos, a video-generation model in a different single-view/prompted setting. No particle-based simulator baselines are reimplemented, despite the paper positioning itself against GNN/kNN PBS methods.

LPIPS results are substantially worse than Cosmos on several datasets (e.g., Rigid: 0.89 vs. 0.24/0.58; Elastic: 0.82-0.83 vs. 0.23/0.87; Cloth: 0.88 vs. 0.19/0.14), which undermines visual-quality claims and suggests possible blurry predictions despite higher PSNR.

All experiments are synthetic, using GSO objects and Genesis MPM simulation; datasets are small (<6 minutes of video per object, six objects). Real-world videos and real-world physics are not evaluated, and the paper acknowledges this as proof-of-concept only.

Generalization claims around scene editing, ground removal, higher throws, and multi-body interactions are supported only qualitatively. There are no controlled quantitative studies, failure-case analyses, or robustness metrics for these settings.

The comparison to Cosmos is not fully apples-to-apples: Cosmos receives language prompts and single-view past frames, while 3DGSim uses calibrated multi-view input. No statistical significance testing is reported.
Reproducibility cannot be verified at review time; code and datasets are promised but not yet available, and training requires a single H100 for ~5 days, limiting independent verification.

The results table contains apparent duplicated rows and inconsistent numbering/reporting (e.g., duplicate 3DGSim 4-12 latent entries in the Elastic table), reducing confidence in experimental reporting.

Claims about avoiding privileged supervision should be qualified: the method still relies on multi-view calibrated cameras, synthetic simulated scenes, and optionally segmentation masks; it is not trained on unconstrained real-world RGB video.
Optional masking/freezing and static-background handling are used in final models but not fully ablated or analyzed for their contribution to the headline dynamics results.

strengths: The paper presents an ambitious end-to-end differentiable framework for learning 3D particle-based simulators directly from multi-view RGB videos, integrating inverse rendering, transformer dynamics, and Gaussian splatting rendering in a single trainable pipeline.

The architectural extensions are technically interesting: the temporal encoding and merging (TEM) module extends PTv3-style point-cloud serialization to spatio-temporal particle sets, enabling reuse of attention blocks across time steps and longer rollouts.

The empirical study covers multiple dynamic regimes (rigid, elastic, cloth) and includes useful ablations showing the importance of TEM, latent versus explicit 3DGS representations, input window length, and rollout length.

The qualitative out-of-distribution experiments, such as ground removal and multi-object interactions, are compelling and support the claim that a 3D particle state can provide better spatial consistency and object permanence than 2D video models.

The paper provides detailed implementation and hyperparameter settings, claims open-source code and dataset release, and reports simulation speed, which is useful for reproducibility and practical adoption.
The limitations section is relatively candid about dependence on multi-view input, occlusion handling, and the tradeoff between 3D spatial causality and generative freedom.
weaknesses: The primary evaluation is image-space reconstruction quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FVD), without quantitative metrics on physical state accuracy, such as particle trajectories, velocities, contact behavior, or material-parameter recovery. The authors argue that particle representations differ from simulators, but this leaves the central claim of learning accurate physical interactions only indirectly validated.

Baseline comparisons are limited and not fully satisfying. The strongest prior learned particle-based simulators are not compared quantitatively due to unavailable code/datasets, Spring-Gaus is not designed for the same task and requires privileged inputs, and Cosmos is a 2D video model, so the experiments do not establish state-of-the-art performance for 3D learned simulators.

The datasets are synthetic, small in scale (six objects per regime, less than six minutes of video per object), and may not capture the diversity needed to substantiate broad claims about scalable visuo-physical simulation. Real-world results are preliminary, use a different inverse-rendering backbone, and are mostly qualitative.

Many ablations are performed only on the elastic dataset, and key hyperparameters such as grid resolution and temporal-merging strides appear tuned on that dataset. Robustness of the conclusions across rigid, cloth, and real-world settings is therefore unclear.

The paper makes strong claims about emergent physical laws, spatial causality, and generalization beyond training distributions, but the evidence is mostly visual rollout quality. There is little probing of latent features, no explicit causal analysis, and no systematic stress-testing of physical consistency.

The method depends on multi-view inputs and known camera parameters, which limits applicability to many real-world domains. The real-world experiment mitigates this with a pretrained monocular depth model, but that changes the pipeline substantially and is not extensively evaluated.

Reproducibility is partially limited by heavy compute requirements (about six days on a single H100) and by baseline unavailability. The claimed code/dataset release is promising but cannot be verified from the manuscript alone.

There are presentation issues in the extracted manuscript, including reference/citation inconsistencies and some important architectural details relegated to the appendix, which slightly hinder readability.

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely novel combination: a fully end-to-end differentiable pipeline that chains feed-forward inverse rendering (MVSplat), a transformer-only point-cloud dynamics model (based on PTv3), and a 3D Gaussian Splatting decoder, jointly trained on an image reconstruction loss. Removing kNN graph construction and hand-crafted edge features in favor of serialization + learned spatiotemporal embeddings is a reasonable and interesting research direction.

The Temporal Encoding & Merging (TEM) mechanism, which encodes a timestamp into a 64-bit serialization code and merges adjacent timesteps via a one-bit right shift, is a clean and memory-efficient way to handle arbitrary-length temporal inputs within the same attention block. The ablation showing removal of TEM collapses performance (~18 PSNR vs 33.15) provides concrete evidence that temporal merging is doing real work, and the merging-stride/embedding ablations (Table S8) are informative.

The quantitative results on elastic and cloth data (e.g., Elastic 33.15 PSNR / 91.3 FVD vs CosmosFT 26.97 / 156.4; Cloth 26.46 vs 23.12) are competitive with, and in some cases better than, a LoRA-finetuned large video model and Spring-Gaus, despite using no privileged depth or object tracks.

The qualitative OOD demonstrations (ground removal, multi-object collisions, emergent shadows) and the real-world HO-Cap rollouts (120 steps, with a stability/failure analysis in Fig. S14-S15) illustrate a plausible advantage of explicit 3D state over 2D video prediction, e.g., avoiding the object 'morphing' and 'levitation' artifacts reported for CosmosFT.
The paper is honest about several limitations (autoregressive drift and hand-particle fading, dependence on multi-view input, inability to create/destroy particles, mask reliance in Section C.3).
weaknesses: The paper's headline claim—that 3DGSim 'learns physical interactions' and produces 'physically plausible' results—is supported almost entirely by image-space metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD) and qualitative figures. Section E explicitly argues against physical-state metrics, but this leaves the central 'learns physics' claim without any physical evaluation (no particle-trajectory error in a common frame, contact/penetration statistics, conservation checks, or comparison of predicted vs. ground-truth simulation state). Good rendering is not evidence of correct dynamics, and the paper does not resolve this gap.

The OOD generalization claims that headline the paper (ground removal, object duplication/multi-body interaction, emergent shadows; Figs. 9-12, S2-S11) are shown only via cherry-picked qualitative rollouts, with no quantitative evaluation, no success/failure rates, and no controlled protocol. For a paper whose main selling point is generalization beyond the training distribution, this is a serious evidential gap.

The baseline comparison is weak in ways that inflate the apparent contribution. Key 3D competitors (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys) are excluded on the grounds of unavailability, which is at best a partial justification. The only learned 2D baseline (CosmosFT) is fine-tuned for just 6,000 iterations, which is unlikely to reflect the model's capability and makes the comparison potentially unfair in favor of 3DGSim. The Spring-Gaus comparison is acknowledged by the authors themselves as 'not fully fair' (per-trajectory optimization and privileged GT ground height/masks), yet is still reported as evidence of superiority.

All three datasets are self-generated simulations (MOVI rigid bodies, Genesis MPM elastic/cloth), so there is no established external benchmark and no independent validation of the claimed difficulty or realism. On the rigid dataset the improvement over CosmosFT is marginal (28.35 vs 27.31 PSNR), undermining the generality of the 'accurate dynamics' claim for the hardest case (rigid bodies).

Presentation quality is poor and would need substantial revision: garbled citations (year mismatches and duplicate 'Whitney et al., 2024' entries without a/b disambiguation; Slotformer cited as Li et al., 2022; DINOv3 as Siméoni et al., 2021; Perez 2017 vs 2021; downs 2022 vs 2024), broken/orphan text (e.g., 'for passive phenomena', 'action conditioning on enable large-scale validation'), inconsistent table references, and undefined hyperparameters (e.g., n_f is never specified). Claims such as 'pioneers an unexplored direction' overstate novelty given prior learned particle simulators from video (VPD/HD-VPD).

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: training takes ~6 days on a single H100 for the synthetic experiments, the code/dataset release is only promised, and several design choices (feature dimensions, explicit vs. implicit representation definitions, variable-length input handling) are under-specified.

The ablation/experimental design mixes confounds (e.g., the 'Modality' and grid-resolution ablations use different training budgets—80k vs 120k steps in Table S8), and the chosen 'best' configuration is not consistent across metrics (3DGSim 2-12 latent has much lower FVD than 4-12 latent but lower PSNR, which is not reconciled).

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: learning 3D particle-based simulators directly from multi-view RGB videos without privileged signals such as depth, object tracks, or hand-crafted graph connectivity. The proposed 3DGSim is a coherent, fully differentiable pipeline combining a MVSplat-based inverse renderer, a PTv3-derived temporal point transformer, and Gaussian splatting for image-space supervision.

The technical extension of PTv3 to spatiotemporal point clouds is novel and well motivated. The temporal encoding/merging (TEM) mechanism via shifted temporal codes and patch grouping is a simple way to reuse attention blocks across timesteps and reduce memory, and the ablation shows removing TEM causes a large collapse (18.19 PSNR vs. 33.15).

The empirical results, while limited, are promising: 3DGSim outperforms strong 2D video baselines (Cosmos/CosmosFT) and Spring-Gaus on future prediction on the authors' rigid, elastic, and cloth datasets; ablations isolate the contributions of latent vs. explicit features, input window length, rollout length, and TEM.

The qualitative generalization examples (ground removal, multi-object interactions, shadows, HO-Cap real-world rollouts) are compelling illustrations of the benefits of an explicit 3D state over 2D video generation, even if they are not quantitative.

Reproducibility appears good: the paper promises code and dataset release, describes architectures and hyperparameters in detail, and reports training time/hardware. Limitations (multi-view dependence, occlusion, particle creation/destruction) are discussed openly.
weaknesses: The central claim 'can we give up graph inductive bias?' is not directly tested against any GNN-based particle simulator on the same data. The paper argues that VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, and 3D-IntPhys are unavailable, but it could have implemented a simple GNN baseline to substantiate the comparison; without this, the main architectural argument is weaker than claimed.

The quantitative evaluation relies on self-generated simulated datasets and image-space metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD). There is no quantitative measurement of physical plausibility, object permanence, collision consistency, or long-horizon dynamics; OOD generalization is demonstrated only qualitatively. This limits support for the claim that the model learns physical interactions rather than image-space continuations.

The 'arbitrary number of timesteps' contribution is overstated. Table S2 shows performance degrades substantially with input windows longer or shorter than the training setup (8 frames: 28.60 PSNR vs. 4 frames: 33.15; 1 frame: 22.92), and the paper notes untrained temporal embeddings corrupt representations. Thus temporal merging does not actually support arbitrary input lengths without retraining or careful matching to training.

Baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. CosmosFT is a 2D language-conditioned video model, and Spring-Gaus requires privileged ground height/masks, performs per-trajectory optimization, cannot handle cloth, and does not model lighting. The authors acknowledge some of this, but the quantitative table remains hard to interpret as a fair assessment of 3D particle-based simulation.

The real-world validation is preliminary, action-conditioned, and uses a pretrained depth model rather than a passive multi-view RGB simulator. It is useful as a qualitative proof of concept but does not establish that the method scales to real-world passive videos as claimed in the abstract/introduction.

The paper lacks training-seed variance or statistical significance analysis for the main results, reporting only trajectory-level standard deviations. This makes it hard to know whether small differences (e.g., 4-step vs. 2-step input) are robust.

Some presentation issues remain: several claims in the abstract/introduction/contributions are stronger than the evidence (e.g., 'arbitrary number of timesteps', 'physically plausible even in out-of-distribution cases'), and there are minor typos and formatting inconsistencies in the appendix tables.
